newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan consults fellow G7 members on Lima crisis.
newsitem.headline: Japan consults fellow G7 members on Lima crisis.

text.p: Japan revealed on Friday it has begun consulting fellow members of the Group of Seven (G7) industrialised nations to hammer out a possible joint solution to the 10-day-old Peru hostage crisis.
Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda told a news conference Japan has started talks with Britain, Germany, France, Italy, Canada and the United States to draft a joint plan to end the drama.
A Foreign Ministry spokesman later said that Japan was also in touch with Russia on the issue.
The move to seek a G7 solution follows a similar proposal by Russian President Boris Yeltsin earlier this week.
Yeltsin sent two letters, one to G7 leaders and another to Peruvian President Alberto Fujimori, calling for adoption of a collective G7 approach to the crisis.

In the letters, he suggested a joint declaration by the G7 plus Russia, offering coordinated moves to resolve the crisis including possible dispatch of anti-terrorist squads and establishment of a joint headquarters to conduct a hostage-freeing operation in Lima.

Peruvian Marxist guerrillas are still holding more than 100 hostages inside the Lima residence of the Japanese ambassador to Peru after storming into the compound during a packed reception on December 17.

"It is clear that the international community should not condone terrorism. It is also necessary for the international community to act as one to help resolve this crisis by setting free all the hostages peacefully, and at an early date," Ikeda said.
"With this in mind, we have already started consultations (with the other G7 member states)."
At the annual summit of G7 leaders in Lyon, France, last July, the world's seven most industrialised nations approved a list of 25 practical measures to defeat terrorism.

The package included pledges to reinforce police cooperation and training, share intelligence, make extradition procedures easier, cut off sources of terrorist funding and weapons, and strengthen national anti-terrorism legislation.

Asked if Lima could be the first test of collective anti-terrorist moves by the G7 and Russia, which attended the Lyon summit as an observer, Foreign Ministry spokesman Hiroshi Hashimoto said it would depend on discussions among members.
"That would depend on the outcome of further consultations among the Group of Seven plus Russia," he said. "At this point it is too early to say what specific measures could be taken."
He added: "In either case, there is no change in Japan's position of complete support for President Fujimori."
